title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the launch pad to the dictionary

questions.prompt: How many words in this sentence contain the sound [ei], the vowel of "space"? — "They paid a great price to reach space."
questions.explanation: The count is 4: they, paid, great and space all carry it. The sound hides behind several spellings — a…e in space, -ai- in paid, -ay- in delay, and even -ea- in the two odd words great and break. The traps here are price, where i…e gives [ai], and reach, where -ea- gives the long [i:] of sea. Never trust the letters alone: say the word aloud and listen for the vowel that ends like the letter y in say.

questions.prompt: An article speaks of "the emerging space-tourism industry". What does "emerging" mean here?
questions.explanation: An emerging industry is one that is appearing and starting to be known: it exists, but the public is only just discovering it. The word comes from to emerge, to come out into view, so it always points to a beginning and never to an end. The idea of joining two things together belongs to merge, which is one letter away, and wealth belongs to well-to-do, another word of this lesson.

questions.prompt: At the meeting, the chief engineer suggested ___ the launch by a week. Which form is correct?
questions.explanation: Suggest is followed by a verb in the -ing form: the engineer suggested delaying the launch. "Suggested to delay" is the mistake nearly every learner makes, because in many languages the idea of proposing something is followed by an infinitive; in English it is not. The bare form would leave two verbs touching with nothing between them, and "to delaying" piles the two patterns one on top of the other.

questions.prompt: You want to say that the guide interrupted the tour in order to answer a phone call. Which sentence says exactly that?

options.text: The guide stopped answering a phone call.
The guide stopped for answering a phone call.
The guide stopped to answer a phone call.
The guide stopped answering to a phone call.

questions.explanation: Only to + infinitive gives the purpose of the interruption: he stopped in order to answer. "Stopped answering" says the opposite — that he had been answering calls and gave that up. "Stopped for answering" borrows a preposition from other languages where English uses to on its own, and to answer to somebody means to be responsible to that person, not to pick up a telephone.

questions.prompt: Complete the series: legal → illegal · regular → irregular · patient → impatient · mature → ___
questions.explanation: The series shows one prefix wearing three faces, and the first letter of the word chooses which one: il- before l, ir- before r, im- before m, p and b. Mature begins with m, so it takes im- and gives immature, exactly as patient gives impatient. Un- and in- do exist, but they never appear before these letters, and non- is kept for words that name an absence rather than an opposite, as in non-smoker.

questions.prompt: A dictionary gives: "foothold (noun) — a first strong position from which you can make progress". Which sentence uses the word as the entry describes it?

options.text: He built a foothold next to the spaceport.
The foothold of the rocket burned on re-entry.
She sold her foothold to a rival company.
The company gained a foothold in China.

questions.explanation: The entry defines a position, not an object: you gain, get or win a foothold, and what you gain is the right to go further — here a first place in the Chinese market from which the company can grow. A position of that kind cannot be built next to a building, cannot burn on re-entry and cannot be sold like a piece of property. The first words of a definition tell you what kind of word you are holding, and "a position" already rules three of these sentences out.
